title: Chalmers’ reforms trigger stampede on super contributions
full_text:
Labor’s capital gains tax crackdown has triggered a stampede into superannuation, with two of the nation’s biggest super funds reporting a 35 per cent surge in voluntary contributions as investors – many over 50 – rush to shelter their wealth from the new tax regime.
Voluntary contributions at the nation’s biggest fund, AustralianSuper, spiked 35 per cent in June compared to the previous June, and continued climbing in July and August, largely from members aged 50-66.
Retail super giant MLC experienced a 35 per cent spike in extra super contributions between May and August compared with the same period last year.
Other retail industry super funds have also seen big increases, and financial planners say more people are considering selling investment properties and funnelling that money into tax-friendly superannuation, an investment pool now worth $4.8 trillion.
In the May budget, Treasurer Jim Chalmers unveiled a ban on negative gearing for established rental properties, and overhauled capital gains taxes in ways that punish long-term property and direct share investors with a top CGT rate of 47 per cent from July 2027.
Superannuation rules have been left largely untouched, apart from Labor’s June announcement to ban self-managed super funds from borrowing money to buy residential property, in a rushed deal it struck with the Greens to secure the minor party’s support for its other tax changes.
MLC’s surge in extra contributions over the past four months is understood to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars. It adds to a broader trend, with the fund noting a 79 per cent rise in contributions since 2024.
MLC chief customer officer Renee Howie said members had been asking more questions about how the recent policy changes might affect them.
“With so much uncertainty around right now, it’s understandable that people are paying closer attention to their finances,” Ms Howie said.
The Financial Services Council says its members have also noticed the shift towards super.
“The government has reduced the attractiveness of other forms of private savings and investment in existing investment properties,” FSC CEO Blake Briggs said.
“Superannuation is now far and away the most attractive investment vehicle for additional savings and wealth creation, next to the family home, due to the government’s new capital gains and trust tax measures announced in the federal budget.” AustralianSuper chief member officer Rose Kerlin said there had been a significant increase in contributions since May.
“Members are increasingly recognising super as a tax-effective opportunity,” she said.
The maximum tax rate in super’s accumulation phase is 15 per cent, and once people retire and shift their money to an account-based pension that tax rate drops to zero per cent on income, capital gains and withdrawals.
Falling property prices across all capital cities in recent months are also reducing real estate’s allure as an investment destination.
Bridges Financial Services financial planner Brenden Maclean said clients who had received inheritances or other windfalls were “not even looking at property now”.
Mr Maclean said the primary feedback he had heard from clients since the budget was “confusion”.
“The rules are changing, and from July 1, 2027 it’s all different,” he said. “They’re a bit scared … people say ‘if I don’t know it I don’t want to touch it’. “Putting money into super is where it’s starting to head.”
